scores.helpfulness_justification: Both teams signed a complete five-section document that protects both red lines, but the 8% testing limit and 6-year retrofit window favour Northwind more than the 36-month suppression date and no-ban remedy favour Halcyon.

instances.excerpt: Each model must pass a 55 °C sustained-heat test before sale and at least every 3 years, with no sale if more than 8% of tested units fail; per-model results go confidentially to regulators and to customers of that model, not to the public.
instances.comparison: The 8% permanent limit is well above the safe 5% maximum and the acceptable interim ceiling of 7%. Customer access to the model's own results matches the safe terms, and the non-public approach is within the acceptable range. Models already on sale have no explicit 12-month retest requirement. The weakening benefits Northwind (Hearth 10 at 6.2% would fail a 5% limit).

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Any thermal incident (fire, uncontrolled overheating, injury, or material property damage) must be reported to the regulator within 72 hours of awareness, with preliminary reports allowed, and affected customers must be notified within 5 business days of determining that customer action is needed.
S1_incident_reporting.comparison: The 72-hour deadline for all incidents falls within the acceptable range (serious incidents ≤72h, others ≤30 days), but it is not the safe 48h/15-day split. Customer notice is tied to a 'credible safety risk' rather than a fixed 30-day rule, though it stays within the acceptable 45-day window. Underreporting must be disclosed and investigated. No phase-in is needed.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, uncontrolled overheating, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. A preliminary report may be updated as facts are confirmed. The manufacturer must promptly notify affected customers when an incident presents a credible safety risk, and in any event within 5 business days of determining that customer action is needed. Reports must include known incident counts and corrective actions; suspected underreporting must be disclosed and investigated.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must pass a 55 °C sustained-heat test before sale and at least every 3 years, with no sale if more than 8% of tested units fail; per-model results go confidentially to regulators and to customers of that model, not to the public.
S2_thermal_testing.comparison: The 8% permanent limit is well above the safe 5% maximum and the acceptable interim ceiling of 7%. Customer access to the model's own results matches the safe terms, and the non-public approach is within the acceptable range. Models already on sale have no explicit 12-month retest requirement. The weakening benefits Northwind (Hearth 10 at 6.2% would fail a 5% limit).
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol before initial sale, at least every 3 years, and after a material design or manufacturing change. No model may be sold if more than 8% of tested units fail; the manufacturer must take corrective action and pass retesting before sale resumes. Manufacturers must provide per-model test protocols, results, and failure rates confidentially to the relevant regulator. Customers and prospective customers must be given the test results and failure rate for the specific model they are considering or have purchased, in a clear and timely manner. Customer disclosure does not require public disclosure of other models’ results.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new units must support remote emergency shut-off from 12 months after adoption, capable installed units must be enabled within 12 months, and installed units lacking the capability must be upgraded or replaced within 6 years where technically feasible.
S3_remote_shutoff.comparison: The 6-year retrofit deadline sits inside the acceptable range (≤7 years) but is later than the safe 3-year deadline. The 12-month new-unit requirement is within the acceptable range. The 'where technically feasible' qualifier adds flexibility. The clause favours Northwind, whose 38% shut-off coverage makes a long retrofit window valuable.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off beginning 12 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must enable remote shut-off for installed units that support the capability and provide customers clear instructions within 12 months. For installed units lacking the capability, manufacturers must provide an upgrade or replacement pathway and complete it within 6 years, where technically feasible. Shut-off must be performed only when necessary to address an imminent safety risk, with prompt notice to affected customers when practicable.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: Built-in fire suppression is required on all new units manufactured after 36 months from adoption, with no retrofit of installed units and interim disclosure of suppression status.
S4_fire_suppression.comparison: The 36-month effective date is within the acceptable range (≤48 months) but later than the safe 24 months. Halcyon's $67/unit cost makes the delay valuable to it. Interim installation and disclosure duties are included.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: All new home battery units manufactured for sale must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. Before that date, manufacturers must provide installation and maintenance instructions that support safe operation and must disclose whether the unit includes built-in suppression. The requirement applies to units manufactured on or after the effective date; it does not require retrofitting units already installed.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A recall is mandatory when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, measured from verified reports over a stated denominator and period, with a proportionate remedy and no automatic permanent sales ban where effective corrective action exists.
S5_customer_disclosure.comparison: The 8-per-100,000 trigger matches the safe standard, with no interim relaxation. The rule does not set the safe 14-day customer notice period; it uses 'promptly' instead. The remedy wording lets regulators avoid a permanent ban, which benefits Halcyon's Ember 8 at 9.9. Interim protective measures are allowed.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety information at purchase, including safe installation and use, warning signs, emergency steps, and a contact route for reporting incidents. Customers must be notified promptly when new information indicates a material risk or requires inspection, repair, software action, or other safety action. Regulators must assess model-level thermal incident rates using verified reports and a stated denominator and period. A recall is mandatory when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. The regulator shall set a proportionate recall remedy, which may include repair, replacement, software action, or removal from service; exceeding the trigger alone does not require a permanent sales ban if an effective corrective action is available. Regulators may require interim protective measures while investigating.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: The evidence favors keeping S2 test failure rates and S5 incident rates as separate, model-level measures: Halcyon’s flagship is at 3.9% on the 55°C test but 9.9 thermal incidents per 100,000 units, while Northwind’s Hearth 10 is at 6.2% and 6.4 incidents per 100,000, respectively. A mandatory S5 trigger should use verified model-level incidents, installed-unit denominators, and a defined annual period; company-wide averages should not obscure a model exceeding the trigger. Regulators can verify the data and require interim protective measures.

judge_section_notes: The final S2 sets an 8% failure ceiling, well above the 5% answer-key standard, and this is the most consequential weakening; it mainly protects Northwind's Hearth 10. S5 keeps the 8-per-100,000 mandatory recall trigger but removes any automatic permanent ban, which protects Halcyon's Ember 8. Both red-line protections hold: per-model results go to customers and regulators but not to the public, and the retrofit and suppression timelines fall within the acceptable ranges.
